overview.main_topic: Interpreting `predict()` output as a 46-way probability distribution, and switching from one-hot labels to integer labels with `sparse_categorical_crossentropy`
overview.central_idea: For each newswire the model returns 46 probabilities summing to 1, and the predicted topic is their argmax. If you keep the labels as integers instead of one-hot vectors, the only change needed is the loss: `sparse_categorical_crossentropy`.
overview.importance: It connects the softmax output to an actual decision (argmax) and clears up a frequent source of shape errors in Keras: matching the loss to the label encoding.

summary:
**4.2.5 Generating predictions on new data.** Calling `model.predict(x_test)` on the trained model returns, for every test newswire, "a class probability distribution over all 46 topics." The authors check three properties on the first test sample:

- `predictions[0].shape` is `(46,)`: one score per topic (so `predictions` as a whole has shape `(2246, 46)`).
- `np.sum(predictions[0])` is `1.0`: the entries form a probability distribution, a consequence of the softmax last layer.
- `np.argmax(predictions[0])` is `4`: the predicted class is the one with the highest probability, here topic 4.

**4.2.6 A different way to handle the labels and the loss.** On p.142 the authors noted two ways to vectorize the labels. Instead of one-hot encoding, you can leave them as integer tensors: `y_train = train_labels`, `y_test = test_labels`. The text says the only thing this changes is the loss function. `categorical_crossentropy`, used in listing 4.22, expects labels in categorical (one-hot) encoding; with integer labels you should use **`sparse_categorical_crossentropy`**, shown in a `compile()` call with Adam and `metrics=["accuracy"]`. The continuation on p.149 adds that the sparse loss is mathematically the same as categorical crossentropy and only has a different interface.

Beyond the book: integer labels are also lighter in memory, a length-2,246 vector instead of a 2,246 × 46 matrix, which matters for problems with many classes (such as the vocabulary-sized outputs of language models later in the book).

paragraphs.excerpt: Calling the model’s predict method on new samples returns a class probability
paragraphs.what_it_says: `predict()` returns a probability distribution over the 46 topics for each input sample, and the authors run it on the whole test set.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The output is a 2-D array of shape (number of samples, 46). Row i holds the model's softmax probabilities for newswire i. Nothing is thresholded or decided yet; the model gives graded beliefs.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: In deployment you call `predict()`, not `evaluate()`: there are no labels for new data, only the model's distribution, which you then turn into a decision.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `predict` runs the forward pass in batches (default 32) without computing gradients or metrics.

terminology.meaning: Keras method that runs the model on inputs and returns its outputs.
A vector of non-negative values, one per class, summing to 1.

connections: p.158: the book contrasts the outputs of predict() for binary, multiclass and regression models.

paragraphs.excerpt: Each entry in “predictions” is a vector of length 46:
paragraphs.what_it_says: Each row of the predictions array has length 46.
paragraphs.what_it_means: One probability per topic, matching the `Dense(46, activation="softmax")` last layer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Checking output shapes is the quickest sanity check that the model is wired as intended.
connections: p.143: the last layer has 46 units, one per class.

paragraphs.excerpt: The coefficients in this vector sum to 1, as they form a
paragraphs.what_it_says: The 46 values sum to 1 because they are a probability distribution.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Softmax exponentiates the 46 logits and divides by their sum, so outputs are positive and normalized. In float32 the sum may show as 1.0 or something like 0.99999994.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It allows you to read `predictions[0][k]` as the model's estimated probability of topic k.

terminology.meaning: Here, the entries of the prediction vector.

paragraphs.excerpt: The largest entry is the predicted class—the class with the highest probability:
paragraphs.what_it_says: The predicted class is the index of the largest probability, found with `np.argmax`; for the first test sample that is class 4.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Turning the distribution into a single label is a separate decision step. Accuracy, as measured during training, is computed exactly this way: argmax of the prediction compared with the true label.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why a model can be confident or unsure yet give the same argmax, which is why accuracy is called a crude metric on p.143.

terminology.meaning: The index of the maximum value in an array.

connections: p.143: top-k accuracy generalizes this to the k largest entries.

paragraphs.excerpt: We mentioned earlier that another way to encode the labels would be
paragraphs.what_it_says: Labels can be kept as integer tensors, simply assigning `y_train = train_labels` and `y_test = test_labels`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each label is the topic index 0-45 stored directly, so `y_train` has shape (8982,) instead of the (8982, 46) one-hot matrix.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It saves the encoding step and memory, and it is the natural format the dataset already comes in (p.141).

terminology.meaning: A tensor of integer class indices, one per sample.

connections: p.142: the two label-encoding options were first introduced with listing 4.14.

paragraphs.excerpt: The only thing this approach would change is the choice of the
paragraphs.what_it_says: With integer labels, the loss must be switched from `categorical_crossentropy` (which expects one-hot labels) to `sparse_categorical_crossentropy`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Both losses compute $-\log$ of the predicted probability of the true class; they differ only in whether the true class is given as a one-hot vector or as an index. The model, optimizer and metrics are unchanged.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Mixing the two is a common error: integer labels with `categorical_crossentropy` raise a shape mismatch (or, with shape (N, 1), are silently misinterpreted), and one-hot labels with the sparse loss fail as well.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Internally the sparse version gathers the log-probability at the label index instead of doing a dot product with a one-hot vector, which is cheaper when there are many classes.

terminology.meaning: Crossentropy loss that takes integer class indices as targets.

connections: p.149: the sparse loss is mathematically the same as categorical crossentropy.
p.150: the wrap-up lists both label/loss pairings.

concepts.name: Softmax output
concepts.definition: An activation that turns a vector of real scores into a probability distribution: positive entries that sum to 1.
concepts.intuition: Exaggerates differences between scores, then normalizes them into shares of 100%.
concepts.significance: Makes `predictions[0]` interpretable as probabilities and makes crossentropy applicable.
concepts.misconception: Softmax probabilities are not guaranteed to be well calibrated; a 0.9 does not necessarily mean 90% of such predictions are correct.

concepts.name: Argmax decision
concepts.definition: Choosing the class with the highest predicted probability.
concepts.intuition: Pick the topic the model believes most.
concepts.technical: `np.argmax(predictions[0])` → 4; for the whole test set, `np.argmax(predictions, axis=1)` gives 2,246 class indices.
concepts.significance: This is how probabilities become labels and how accuracy is computed.
concepts.example: If probabilities for classes 3, 4 and 19 are 0.2, 0.6, 0.1, argmax is 4.
concepts.misconception: Argmax discards confidence: 0.26 and 0.99 on the winning class give the same decision.

concepts.name: Sparse categorical crossentropy
concepts.definition: The crossentropy loss for integer class labels.
concepts.intuition: Same penalty as categorical crossentropy, but you say "the answer is class 3" rather than handing over a 46-long vector with a 1 at index 3.
concepts.technical: $\mathcal{L} = -\log \hat y_{c}$ with $c$ the integer label; identical to categorical crossentropy with one-hot $y$.
concepts.significance: Lets you skip one-hot encoding; standard when the number of classes is large.
concepts.misconception: That it is a different (e.g., approximate) loss. It is mathematically the same, only the interface differs (p.149).

concepts.name: One-hot (categorical) encoding
concepts.definition: Representing a class index as an all-zero vector with a 1 at that index.
concepts.intuition: A row of 46 switches with exactly one turned on.
concepts.technical: Reuters labels become shape (8982, 46) with `to_categorical` or the custom `one_hot_encode` (p.142).
concepts.misconception: One-hot labels do not carry more information than integers; they are just another format.

math.title: Predicted class from the probability vector

variables.meaning: Softmax output for one sample, `predictions[0]`, length 46
Predicted topic index (4 for the first test sample)

math.operations: Sum of the entries (normalization check) and index of the maximum entry (decision).
math.purpose: Formalizes the three REPL checks of section 4.2.5.
math.interpretation: The predicted topic is the most probable one under the model.
math.intuition: The probabilities are a vote; argmax picks the winner.
math.numerical_example: If $\hat y_4 = 0.62$, $\hat y_3 = 0.20$ and the other 44 entries share 0.18, then $\hat c = 4$ and the sum is 1.

math.title: Sparse and categorical crossentropy are the same quantity
math.operations: The left side sums over all classes but only one term is nonzero; the right side indexes that term directly.
math.purpose: Shows why the book can say only the loss name changes and (on p.149) that the two losses are mathematically equivalent.
math.interpretation: Same value, same gradients, different label format.
math.intuition: Multiplying by a one-hot vector is just a lookup.

pitfalls: Any metric that expects one-hot targets (e.g., `TopKCategoricalAccuracy`) must be swapped for its sparse version (`SparseTopKCategoricalAccuracy`).

deeper.title: Matching label format to loss: a quick table
deeper.body:
| Label format | Shape (Reuters train) | Loss | Accuracy metric Keras uses |
|---|---|---|---|
| one-hot | (8982, 46) | `categorical_crossentropy` | categorical accuracy |
| integer | (8982,) | `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` | sparse categorical accuracy |

Note (not in the book): Keras picks the right accuracy variant automatically when you pass the string `"accuracy"`, based on the loss and target shapes.

deeper.title: Why sparse labels scale better
deeper.body: Beyond the book: one-hot labels for a 50,000-token vocabulary and a batch of 64 sequences of 100 tokens would need $64\cdot100\cdot50{,}000 = 320$ million floats, whereas integer labels need 6,400 integers. This is why language models (chapter 15, p.449) are trained with sparse crossentropy.

questions.question: What is the shape of `predictions = model.predict(x_test)` for the Reuters model?
questions.explanation: There are 2,246 test samples and 46 outputs per sample. (46,) is one row, (2246,) would be argmax labels, and (2246, 10000) is the input.

questions.question: Why does `np.sum(predictions[0])` return 1.0?
questions.answer: Because the last layer uses softmax, whose outputs are a probability distribution summing to 1.
questions.explanation: The book states the coefficients form a probability distribution (p.148), following from the softmax layer described on p.143.

questions.question: You set `y_train = train_labels` (integers) but keep `loss="categorical_crossentropy"`. What is the problem?
options: The categorical loss expects one-hot labels, so the targets do not match the (batch, 46) predictions
The model must have an integer output layer
Accuracy cannot be computed with integer labels
questions.answer: The categorical loss expects one-hot labels, so the targets do not match the (batch, 46) predictions
questions.explanation: The book says categorical_crossentropy expects categorical encoding; with integers you should use the sparse loss. Keras does not convert automatically, the model is unchanged, and accuracy works fine with integer labels and the sparse loss.

questions.question: A prediction vector has 0.55 on topic 4 (the true topic). Compute the loss under both categorical crossentropy (one-hot label) and sparse categorical crossentropy (label 4).
questions.explanation: With a one-hot label only the true-class term survives the sum, so both losses reduce to −log of the true-class probability.

questions.question: Two models output 0.26 and 0.95 respectively on topic 4 for the same sample (topic 4 being the largest entry in both). How do their accuracies and losses on this sample compare?
questions.answer: Accuracy is identical (both argmax = 4), but the loss is much higher for the first model (−ln 0.26 ≈ 1.35 vs. −ln 0.95 ≈ 0.05).
questions.explanation: Argmax ignores confidence; crossentropy does not. This is why the loss and accuracy curves can behave differently.

questions.question: How would you get the predicted topic for every test sample at once?
questions.answer: `np.argmax(predictions, axis=1)`, which returns an array of shape (2246,).
questions.explanation: The page shows argmax for one row; `axis=1` applies it along the class axis of every row (AI extension).

questions.question: Without looking, can you state which loss goes with one-hot labels and which with integer labels, and what shapes those labels have for Reuters training data?
questions.explanation: This pairing is the core of section 4.2.6 and is repeated in the wrap-up on p.150.
